There is no matter here to receive a new form, as wax receives the shape of a square. Giving an image a specific identity is not a second act added to its creation. The defining feature follows from the image itself.
This is like the forms of the afterlife, which do not have the place and position found in this world.

Changes in the next world do not happen because matter takes on one form after another. There is no matter there. Changes such as new skins or new kinds of pleasure come from one creation followed by another. The details will be discussed in the sections on the afterlife.
When an imagined form disappears, it does not turn into something else that can serve as its matter. It simply ceases to be. This is different from material things, which change into something else.
The distinction between images in the world of imagination does not mean they have positions in the physical world. This note corrects the wording of the sentence it follows.

The relation is part of what makes a particular instance what it is; it is not an added thing alongside it. If the relation were an extra object, the difference between the general kind and the particular instance would not be only a matter of thought. This also challenges the argument that estimation perceives a compound of meaning and image. If you ask how estimation can link a meaning to an image without knowing the image, the answer is like saying that Zayd is a human being: it is not a real joining of two separate things. The image is perceived by imagination; the particular meaning is perceived by intellect linked to imagination, or by estimation in the usual account. The relation makes it particular.

Hostility joined to a particular image is not one single thing. It is perceived by intellect working with imagination, not by intellect connected to imagination alone. This also challenges the argument just given.

The power of resolve is the firm wish of practical reason, such as deciding to visit someone who is ill. Animal desire is the firm wish of the bodily motive power, such as visiting someone for personal gain. In a human being, theoretical and practical reason play roles like perception and movement in an animal. The higher source of an inclination is called will or love; the animal source is called appetite. Religious language also distinguishes them. Mystics sometimes use “love” of God and the soul, though prophets usually teach with simpler, proper terms.

The author identifies will with the power that wills, as he identifies knowledge with the one who knows. Both estimation and imagination are immaterial, but estimation is at a higher level. The note that no one calls the power that urges action material is meant as a small exception to praise, a familiar figure of speech.
The philosophers’ classification of ability as a mental quality supports the author’s account that the soul is one through all its levels, reaching into the body.
The working power spreads through the body much like nature does. It acts through the muscles and limbs, while nature acts through simple and complex bodies.

These thinkers may have spoken about life without separating it into perception and movement. Yet they did, in effect, understand animal life through both. Those who followed the path of life also included perception and movement in their account, but did not treat them as separate paths.

This can be read as “a substance moved by itself,” or as meaning that the soul is a self-moving substance. In the author’s interpretation, this means the changing nature that is one level of the soul.

The copies I have seen read this way, though I cannot check Avicenna’s text now. “And some said” would be a clearer transition: those who did not avoid calling the soul a body divided into several groups, including those who said it was made of indivisible particles.

Here “source” means the source of the world, though some thinkers made it a source only through the first source, God. Thales of Miletus is said to have called water the first element, containing the forms of everything that exists or could exist. From it, earth formed by thickening and freezing, while fire and air formed by thinning. The sky, some said, came from smoke rising from fire. A story attributed to the Torah says that God created a substance, looked upon it, and its parts melted into water. Vapor rose from the water and formed the heavens; foam appeared on its surface and formed the earth and mountains. Similar stories appear in reports from the Imams. Other thinkers said that earth came first, or that air did, becoming fire when thin and earth when dense. Some named fire or vapor as the first source. Anaxagoras spoke of a mixture. Democritus proposed small, hard particles in an endless empty space. Dualists said light and darkness were the world’s two roots. Some Iranian thinkers proposed five eternal things: God, soul, matter, time, and empty space. The Pythagoreans said numbers came from unity and were the source of things.

These views are false if taken literally, though many can be understood in a better way. Their argument can be set out like this: the soul perceives other things; anything that perceives other things is a source; every source is fire, air, earth, or water; so the soul is one of these. The same pattern lies behind the other views.

These thinkers counted the four elements as the roots of the world’s coming to be and continuing to exist. The world arises from them, while its survival depends on drawing what is useful and driving away what is harmful, through what they called Love and Strife.
These thinkers treated life as their route to the soul, and explained it through what gives life, supports it, prepares for it, or follows from it.

For these thinkers, the soul changes only in its qualities: it gains more knowledge, power, and similar features, while its underlying nature remains fixed. The author’s view is different. Through substantial movement, the soul itself changes in its being, while one underlying thread remains from its beginning to its end. This follows from his view that existence is what is real, and that what makes a thing distinct from others is the same as what makes it continuous through change. So the soul’s level as a potential intellect and its level as an actual intellect belong to one changing soul.

The difference between a Prophet and the rest of the community is therefore a difference in the soul’s being, not merely in outside qualities. If such a difference exists within one soul, the difference between two souls may be greater still—like the difference between spirit and body, or between the spirit that gives itself up in the light of the One and the body it leaves behind.

In this account, every earlier form becomes like the material for the final, most complete form. The final form gathers and completes what came before. At the inner level, individuals of the human kind may therefore differ as kinds: some are intellects only in possibility, others are intellects in reality. The rising intellects relate to the final, perfected intellect as earlier forms relate to the final form. In one sense, they are that intellect, and it is them. The author points to sayings about the Prophet and the Imams: “You are remembered among those who remember; your names among the names; your selves among the selves; your spirits among the spirits; your bodies among the bodies.” He also cites the saying that a believer is a mirror for another believer.

The author has briefly pointed to the Prophet’s spiritual reality as the highest completion, for whose sake the rest was created. In this spiritual aspect, no angel or prophet equals him, since every soul and intellect comes from that source. He then turns to the Prophet’s ordinary human life, where likeness and comparison apply. A true knower must hold together both levels: the image and the meaning, the human form and its spiritual reality. The Qur'an says, “If We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man,” to avoid both exaggerating his status and denying the high rank of holy souls.

What is said about the Prophets and Imams—their purity and their likeness to God—is true of their spiritual aspect. What is said about their human limits is also true of their bodily aspect. They eat, drink, sleep, and receive knowledge from Gabriel, because all their gifts come from God. Yet the body’s physical nature is overwhelmed by their spiritual nature. This is why it is said that the Prophet cast no shadow, saw behind him, and that the body of a believer does not decay.

Even a heavenly body, considered only as a body, can perish. The source of its motion is its soul or nature, which is outside the body when “body” means matter considered on its own. The soul and nature are not outside the body when body is considered together with its form.

The soul’s original nature must lead it toward its goal. Otherwise, this natural drive would be pointless. The goal of living souls is something lasting: God and the immaterial intellects, or the world of imagined and estimative forms. These remain through God’s lasting existence.

Movement can be divided into six kinds. Three begin from outside the moving thing: movement through place may begin because something is uncomfortable; the changes in mixed bodies depend on outside heat, cold, or moisture; and the movement of simple elements depends on the conditions around them. The changing nature within a body also moves by itself, but the conflicting elements destroy one another. The other three kinds are the movements of souls. They come from within and do not conflict with one another, so they continue.

The sphere stands for the simple shape of imagined bodies. Its roundness is also explained by the way soul and body are joined as form and matter. Here “body” means a heavenly body, not an imaginal body.

This seems to conflict with the earlier claim that the particles breathed in are imaginal forms, since breathing brings in the bodily vital spirit. The reply is that the vital spirit carries the powers and displays the imaginal forms. Without it, the soul’s image would have no bodily appearance. So refreshing the vital spirit also refreshes the forms it carries.

A clearer reading is that the earlier thinkers meant imaginal bodies by “indivisible spheres,” while by what is breathed in they meant the vital spirit. They may instead have followed the theory of small, hard particles.
This explains the “fire with three branches”: a body has length, width, and depth. The author also links the body’s attachment to the natural world with the fire of punishment in the next life.

There is another way to interpret the number sequence. The first source is one and has no separate definition beyond its unity. From it comes the first intellect, which has two aspects: existence and essence. From that comes the soul, which has a third relation, its direction toward and care for matter. From the soul comes nature, which adds a fourth relation: being present in and acting directly on matter. This completes the active sources.

Potential intellect is like the matter of ideas, and sense is like the matter of sensible forms. Each is suited to receive its own kind, just as silver is suited to take the shape of what is made from it.

The soul does not become one with an object merely because the object is seen or understood indirectly. It becomes one with the form it directly perceives. This does not mean that the soul is made up of many parts. The forms it knows are present through the soul’s own being. As the soul becomes more complete, it gathers more things while becoming more simple.

This differs from the usual view of philosophers and natural scientists, who say that the vital spirit is made from the finest bodily fluids. The body’s organs, they say, are made from the thicker fluids. The author’s view is like his account of food: some things come from the soul itself, or from a natural power that obeys the soul. Other bodily powers may resist it and cause fatigue.

The soul is nourished by ideas and grows stronger through them. When its life appears in the body, bodily things nourish and strengthen that life. The soul rises toward the highest realm until it can stand before God. In the body, its power appears as growth, movement, and reproduction. Each soul helps produce another like itself, so life continues. In this way, all forms in the lower world are shadows of lights and qualities in the higher world.

The source of all things has three levels: God, the existence that flows from Him, and the limited forms that result. The source itself is beyond being a substance or a quality. Earlier thinkers may have meant that God is present in things through His action, not as a separate thing alongside them. Since His action is His command and light, they spoke as if He were nature, soul, or intellect in each thing. But care is needed: each level must be kept distinct and placed in its proper role.
Here “source” means the thing that gives a movement, not a second object of a verb.

The point is that every moving thing needs a source, but not always in the same way. A change in an outer feature needs something to cause that movement. A change in the thing’s very being needs something to give it existence. In this kind of movement, the changing being itself is its movement; the source does not first make it exist and then add movement to it. In outward movement, the source gives the thing existence and also causes the added movement. In either case, all movement needs a source, and the chain of moving things ends at a source that does not move.
The word “change” here is used broadly. In the usual terms, it means change in quality. Change in a thing’s substance is called coming-to-be, as explained earlier.

Substantial movement does not mean that a thing’s definition changes at every moment. Avicenna treats a changing essence as if it became an entirely different kind of thing at each moment. But the definition can remain fixed while the thing’s existence flows and changes. The whole natural world, from the heavens down to the earth, is renewed in its being. This is how the author joins the changing nature of the world with the claim that its definitions do not change.

The movement must be one individual existence unfolding through time; otherwise, there could be no gradual change. Its definition can remain one, like the definition of a human being, even though that definition is expressed through many distinct beings.
Separate intellects do not change. They are complete and do not wait to become something else. Change is possible in kinds of substance that depend on matter.

The highest general kind, such as substance, does not turn into another general kind. Nor does a specific kind of substance turn into another kind during ordinary gradual change. But many kinds of change can take a thing beyond its kind: a color may weaken until it is no longer that color, and a human soul may develop until it becomes angel-like or decline until it becomes devil-like or beast-like.

When the mind is only potential intellect, it receives ideas. When it connects with the active intellect, it can create and preserve them. Or “receiving” may simply mean that the soul is described as having an idea; on either reading, one thing does not have to be both receiver and creator in the same way.

The two parts can each be understood because the condition for understanding applies to them; the whole cannot be understood in that way once the condition is missing. The contrast may be between the whole before division and a part afterward, or between their identities and their accidental features. Either way, if understanding required division, it would require the opposite of what it needs.
If understanding depended on division, then every intelligible thing would have to be divisible. But some intelligible things are simple and cannot be divided.

A part of a magnitude is one particular portion of it, while a particular thing can carry its whole kind. The two objections here may be one or two arguments. Either way, if a smaller part were enough to contain the form, the supposed form would be present with features unrelated to what it is. It would always be understood together with something that does not help complete its meaning.

The questioner points to a mistaken reversal: every division into measured parts gives similar parts, but not every division into similar parts is a division of size. Dividing a universal into its particular kinds is an example.

The phrase about adding “rational” to “animal” may sound as if human and horse natures differ, even though the questioner says their animal nature is the same. The reply is that adding a different feature forms a new kind; it does not split one reality into physical pieces. A universal kind is never found outside its particular instances as one separate thing. Even in the mind, its divisions are made by considering it in different ways. If it were literally divided, its parts would have size.
This would also require an accident to move from one subject to another.

These souls may not yet understand in a fully intellectual way, but they have a capacity close to understanding. If divine care gives them a true intellectual form, they must be ready to receive it, since gifts follow the recipient’s capacity.

Most people cannot understand a universal as a purely intellectual existence, shared equally by many instances. They picture it as an extended thing covering its instances, much as they picture existence as a beam of light. This comes from the strength of imagination and the weakness of their developing intellect. People trained in theory or practice can correct these images with reason. For many, “immaterial” means only that something is not material; a few understand it as a nature stripped of all accompanying features.

The author’s account seems to distinguish three things: a particular idea perceived by sense or imagination; a universal in the strict philosophical sense; and an indeterminate idea that can be considered in different ways. Philosophers usually mean the second when they speak of universals. If minds genuinely understand a universal that is free of particular limits, this understanding is immaterial, though immateriality itself has degrees. The author’s account may deny ordinary people the highest degree of this understanding, but it cannot deny that universal ideas exist in our minds.

The argument moves from number to other realities and then to intellectual forms. The fact that ten can be divided does not prove that other things, especially intellectual forms, can be divided. Ten is divisible because it is a multitude of units; bodies are divisible because they have matter. The argument concerns universal ten as understood by the intellect, not an endless series of individual tens.
Ten is not identical with the many units that compose it, though it can be understood as made up of them. Its meaning as a number includes unity.

The problem with Avicenna’s claim about multitude and unity has already been discussed. In his examples, unity itself includes the multiplicity of parts. That is why some philosophers say that division belongs to the thing represented, not to the feature that represents it.

If “division” means actual separation, the body itself is not what is divided; matter is. If it means division in thought, magnitude is what is directly divisible, and the body is divisible through it.

Even if body and unity refer to one thing, they do not have the same features. A body exists and produces effects; its unity is what rules out division and generality. Different descriptions of one thing can carry different features. The better reply is that, if unity is only a way we consider a thing, it does not literally reside in the body.

Self-knowledge may be direct: the self is both what knows and what is known. Or it may be knowledge through an image. If so, the image is either a likeness, a mere trace, or a description made from features and effects. The respondent rejects some of these options, but the answer does not rule out knowing oneself through one’s features. The clearest answer is that we know our particular self directly, as the “I” we point to; any other image or description is different from that identity.

Here, “awareness is the effect itself” treats the word “awareness” as the form present in the mind. The wording is a technical point: if awareness is the same as the effect, the next phrase adds nothing.
This assumes that “by” means “because of.” The question is whether awareness is the self’s presence itself or a separate awareness caused by an effect.

Avicenna’s point is that our own self is present through its individual identity and nature. The active intellect, by contrast, is present to us only through its nature, not as that individual being. This is direct knowledge of ourselves, but knowledge of the active intellect through an idea.

I think the reply is sound, given its assumptions: separate intellects have distinct natures, and we can know them through concepts. Knowledge through a concept differs from direct awareness, which is the very presence of what is known. A possible being's nature remains recognisable across its different ways of existing. We may therefore understand and define that nature even when we cannot fully grasp the thing's particular existence.

The intellect can understand not only general kinds but also immaterial individuals. Knowing a separate intellect's kind, however, is not the same as possessing that intellect's own individual existence. The same nature can be present in our minds as an intelligible form without becoming the very separate being we know. Its kind may have only one individual outside the mind; that does not prevent its nature from being understood by another mind.

A similar distinction applies when we know God through His names and attributes. We can form ideas that truly point to Him—for example, that He is existence without limitation, simple and undivided, knowing all things through Himself, and fully powerful. Such ideas express what the names mean. They are not God's own existence present in our minds. Just as God's reality is existence itself, so the concept of existence can serve, in our thought, somewhat as an essence serves for a possible being. The divine names and attributes can also play that role. A concept may be general even if its real object cannot be multiplied: the mind can consider several instances of what in fact has only one.

It is true that members of one material kind differ through matter and its features. But what receives a form need not always be a material body. In the case of intellects, the knowing mind is the receiver. Two minds can therefore share knowledge of one nature without becoming one individual intellect. That is a different question from whether what is understood is itself a substance.

If, instead, we reject conceptual knowledge of the intellects and allow only direct awareness of them, the situation changes. Then many souls could be directly aware of one and the same intellect. Their awareness would not be many separate copies of it, because in direct awareness what is known is present rather than represented by another image. Yet direct knowledge itself comes in degrees: the soul's awareness of itself when its intellect is only a possibility is not the same as the awareness it reaches when its intellect is fully developed and, in knowing itself, it knows its Lord.

Nor should we be satisfied with loose, general descriptions of the intellects. We can identify the first intellect as an immaterial substance, the first thing produced by God, the cause of the second intellect, or the object sought by the soul of the highest sphere. Someone might say these are only effects, not the intellect's nature. But the reply is that they point to the inner principle from which those effects follow, just as a human being's distinctive nature is the source of reasoning and speech rather than simply those acts themselves. — س ره

One might say that the self causes its powers and so can know them, while a power cannot fully know what causes it. The reply is that the questioner only asks for the kind of self-awareness that estimation could provide, and estimation can provide that much.
The example is the active intellect. This restates the earlier question more broadly: estimation, too, could serve as a mirror through which the self becomes aware of itself.
A third possibility is that you know yourself directly while knowing Zayd’s soul through an image.

The idea of Zayd’s humanity is joined to your own self, but does not appear twice in you. The one image is known directly as your own self and considered in another way in relation to Zayd. Humanity considered as universal is not an essential part of your self; what is essential is the particular self itself.
The objection concerns the original step in the proof: that self-understanding must mean the self itself is present to itself.

The phrase “exists in itself” does not clearly support the three meanings the questioner assigns to it. The text may instead mean “is not present in something else,” as whiteness is in a body. The later version of this argument lists only two meanings: existing without dependence on something else, and being related to itself.
Animal souls appear in two ways: as their own living presence, connected with the heart’s vital spirit, and as an image in the brain, where the power of estimation is located.

The strongest part of an animal’s soul is its power of desire, which includes appetite and anger and is connected with the heart’s vital spirit. In animals, the heart serves desire. A complete animal soul can survive in an imaginal form after death and, when perfected, its meaning can join the kind of soul to which it belongs.

The reply does not quite follow the first argument. That argument says universal ideas are indivisible, so their perceiver must be immaterial. Here, the reply distinguishes human self-awareness from animal self-awareness: human beings can understand their self apart from bodily features, while animals perceive themselves mixed with other things. But the author’s own view is that animals directly perceive themselves in an imaginal way. That is why he says the reply turns back to the first proof, even though it does not establish the same point in exactly the same way.

Avicenna may mean that understanding the self apart from bodily features is direct awareness of one’s own identity, not understanding one’s universal nature. On that reading, the reply does not change to a different argument.

The questioner is now arguing that animal souls are immaterial. The author agrees with the basic point, in keeping with his account of complete animals, and answers only the weakest part of the objection.

A living being has a soul, and the organ contains an image that corresponds to that soul. The reply compares the image in the organ to reflected green color; it does not itself make the organ alive. If the argument is that the soul and its organ depend on each other, the dependence is different: the soul prepares the organ, while the soul gives it life.
“Present in the organ” means that the soul is what makes the organ actually alive. The soul’s image in the organ is not merely an effect of that life.

The first argument says that universal ideas are indivisible, so their place must be immaterial. This argument says that a universal idea has no particular feature, so its place must have none either. The two arguments are closely related.

In standard philosophical terminology, an “accident” includes not only ordinary qualities but also the category of substance as it exists in the mind. The author, however, treats intellectual universals as immaterial lights or divine forms. A universal can be immaterial and still shared by material individuals: its nature is present in them in a weaker way. This is a different kind of sharing from several people having the same bodily object.

The author’s distinctive claim is that what makes an idea an individual also makes it universal. This is as striking as the claim attributed to Aristotle that what makes opposites alike can also keep them apart.

The idea’s wide intellectual existence lets it apply to many things. Its nature by itself is neither universal nor particular, but it can be applied to many. Applying a concept to many things is a way of thinking about it, not an extra object inside it.

By a “pure human being” the author does not mean the bare idea of human nature emptied of everything, even existence. He means the full intellectual reality of a human being, free from all that is alien to it: boundaries, defects, and limitations. It has none of what does not belong to human reality, and contains everything that does belong to it. As the verse says, “It is no strange thing for God to gather a world in one.”

Although that reality embraces all the countless human individuals found outside the mind or considered within it, it remains one simple reality. Matter and its conditions—place, time, and the like—are what make the individuals many. Once those limiting conditions are removed, the general reality is not divided by them.

Consider whiteness without referring it to this object or that object, this time or that time. Taken simply as whiteness, it is one. So it is with the pure intellectual reality of humanity: we cannot distinguish separate examples inside what is pure in this way.

All these simple and undivided realities resemble, in their own lesser ways, the simple truth and unity of existence itself, which is the most complete of all. The author specifies particular bodily position because there is no problem with a more general concept of position being applied at the intellectual level, as he will argue later when responding to al-Ṭūsī.

The “parts” here are intellectual powers that fulfill the role of bodily organs. The eye’s essential power is sight; the hand’s is the power to grasp. At the highest level, all such powers are one. In lower forms, their differences reappear.
The author means that most people imagine commonality and likeness rather than grasping a universal intellectually.
The commentator disagrees with the examples: recognizing what individuals have in common is an act of intellect, not merely sense or imagination.

“Unlimited” here means that the intellect can keep understanding more without reaching a final limit. Bodily and imaginative powers cannot grasp this endlessness as such; they can picture only a bounded number of images. The intellect may even understand an infinite number of instances in one act, since the nature it considers is one, though the instances are many.
A thing’s ability to be affected cannot be separated from its ability to act: if it exists, it can act, just as it can be affected.

Calling prime matter “eternal” confuses what is true in the mind with what exists outside it. In the world, matter changes along with the forms it receives; it is connected when the form is connected and divided when the form is divided.
On the theory of substantial change, each bodily power is limited in what it can do and what it can undergo. The “new qualities” are changing states, such as successive acts of understanding.

This means the image imprinted in the organ of the intellect—the body that contains the intellectual power. This follows from the assumptions that perception through an organ requires the form in that organ, and that a bodily power uses its bodily subject as its tool.
The second part of the proof is a conditional argument: it joins one statement to an either-or claim, then rejects both alternatives.

The author has already addressed this point. Even so, his objection still works: on his account, the bodily instruments do not themselves perceive. His wording is brief, but the premise is rejected either way.

The objection may be that a form is present in the soul as its source, even if it is not imprinted in the bodily tool. But if bodily powers are imprinted in matter, as many philosophers claim, then the form should be present in their organ.
